newsitem.title: POLAND: Poles begin voting in referendum on constitution.
newsitem.headline: Poles begin voting in referendum on constitution.

text.p: Poles started to vote on Sunday in a referendum to choose between adopting a new constitution, sponsored by the ruling ex-communists, or heeding calls from the powerful rightist opposition to reject it.

Polling stations opened at 6.00 a.m. (0400 GMT) and were due to close at 10.00 p.m. (2000 GMT) -- with first indications of the outcome from exit polls to be announced a few minutes later and the official verdict due late Monday or Tuesday.
The constitution is meant to enshrine rights and liberties the country gained with the fall of communist rule in 1989 and to stabilise the democratic changes made since then.

It has been co-authored by two parliamentary opposition parties descended from the pre-1989 Solidarity movement's fight for democracy, in a compromise with the ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) and its Peasant allies in government.
The Solidarity trade union and allied parties urged voters to reject the document, saying it fails to reflect Poland's Catholic heritage, guarantee sovereignty or settle communist-era wrongs.

The union-led Solidarity Election Action (AWS) alliance, now underrepresented in parliament but rivalling the SLD for first place in opinion polls before elections due in September, is angry the constitution is being pushed through just now.
Union leader Marian Krzaklewski said that to pass what he termed this atheistic constitution just before the election altered the political scene, would "place a time bomb under Poland."
In a last televised address late on Friday, before a pre-vote ban on campaigning took effect, President Aleksander Kwasniewski urged Poles to adopt the new fundamental law.
"This is a good constitution, worthy of our past, allowing us to do justice to our national aspirations," said Kwasniewski, a former communist turned social democrat.
Above all, he urged Poles to take part in the referendum.
Opinion polls suggest voters, baffled by the 243-article document and conflicting accounts from politicians about what it means, may stay away in large numbers.
The vote will be binding no matter how low the turnout, but low participation could mean the battle will continue as the right could argue the new document does not have clear support.

A "no" verdict in the referendum would leave Poland with the vestiges of its discredited 1952 constitution, amended by makeshift 1992 interim laws, until some future parliament can agree enough to pass a new alternative version.
The unwieldy new constitution broadly retains the current political system while weakening the presidency -- a move condemned by former president Lech Walesa.
In economic affairs it sets caps on government spending but obliges it to support employment and home building.
Controversy has centred on visions of national identity.

Solidarity, seeing Poland's history as bound up with the majority Catholic faith, wanted the charter to clearly invoke God, place religious values above man-made law and include a clause effectively banning abortion -- now legal in Poland.
The bishops, greatly concerned over abortion, have announced deep moral reservations about the current document.

The right also says a section permitting Poland by treaty to surrender some functions to international organisations -- designed to ease its entry into the European structures -- unacceptably limits national sovereignty.
The constitution's authors reject these arguments as ill-founded or false and especially on the religious issues they say the document embraces people of all faiths or none.

Although opinion polls have suggested the constitution will pass, the voting may give extra clues to party sympathies ahead of the election and indicate attitudes towards the Church just before a May 31-June 10 visit by Polish Pope John Paul ll.
Solidarity spokesman Piotr Zak said this month his grouping would not be devastated if the constitution passed and would see it as a defeat only if the voting was three to one.
